# Bottom line

- In early rheumatoid arthritis, adding sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine to methotrexate (triple therapy) modestly reduces radiographic progression versus methotrexate alone, but the effect is small and not consistently superior to biologic therapy in head-to-head randomized trials. <cite id="25992914">In SWEFOT, radiographic progression at 24 months was reduced in triple therapy and anti-TNF add-on compared with methotrexate monotherapy, but anti-TNF was marginally superior</cite>. <cite id="27571502,27102806">Network meta-analyses show triple therapy reduces radiographic progression versus methotrexate, but effects are generally small over one year</cite>. <cite id="23755969">In non-responders to methotrexate, triple therapy is noninferior to etanercept plus methotrexate for clinical outcomes, with no significant between-group differences in radiographic progression</cite>.

# Evidence in early disease (triple therapy vs methotrexate monotherapy)

- Randomized trial (SWEFOT): After 24 months, radiographic progression was reduced versus methotrexate monotherapy, but anti-TNF (infliximab) showed a marginal advantage. <cite id="25992914">Observed progression was reduced by 50.1% in triple therapy, 72.3% in anti-TNF, and 73.9% in methotrexate at 12 months; at 24 months, reductions were 87.2% (triple), 89.8% (anti-TNF), and 87.8% (methotrexate), with anti-TNF marginally superior to triple therapy</cite>. <cite id="23497111">DXR-based hand bone loss and subsequent radiographic progression were higher in non-responders, and triple therapy patients had intermediate progression compared with monotherapy</cite>.

- Network meta-analyses: <cite id="27571502,27102806">Across trials, methotrexate plus sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine ("triple therapy") was statistically superior to methotrexate for inhibiting radiographic progression in naïve patients, but mean annual Sharp score changes remained below the minimal clinically important difference over one year</cite>. <cite id="27571502">Biologic combinations (e.g., anti-TNF) were also superior to methotrexate for radiographic outcomes, though effects were small</cite>.

# Head-to-head comparisons relevant to early RA

- Triple therapy vs anti-TNF add-on: <cite id="25992914">In SWEFOT, anti-TNF add-on reduced progression more than triple therapy at 24 months, confirming a marginal advantage for biologics in preventing joint damage</cite>. <cite id="23755969">In a separate randomized trial of methotrexate non-responders, triple therapy was noninferior to etanercept plus methotrexate for DAS28 and secondary outcomes, including radiographic progression</cite>. <cite id="27607411">A POPeRA subanalysis of FIN-RACo/NEO-RACo showed combination therapy versus monotherapy reduced predicted progression over 2–5 years, and anti-TNF induction further improved outcomes, particularly in RF-positive patients</cite>.

# Interpretation for early RA and practical implications

- For early, treatment-naïve RA, triple therapy yields small but statistically detectable radiographic benefits over methotrexate alone, and may be comparable to biologic intensification in real-world practice. <cite id="27571502,27102806">Triple therapy reduces radiographic progression versus methotrexate, though mean changes are modest</cite>. <cite id="25992914">Biologic intensification (anti-TNF) may offer slightly greater radioprotection at 24 months</cite>.

- Clinical decision-making should consider that radiographic gains may be small and not always clinically meaningful, and that adverse events and patient comorbidities influence choice. <cite id="27571502">Triple therapy had fewer withdrawals for adverse events than some biologic combinations and was generally well tolerated</cite>. <cite id="23755969">No significant differences in major adverse events were noted between triple therapy and etanercept plus methotrexate</cite>.

# Answer to the question

- Yes, in early rheumatoid arthritis, initiating combination conventional DMARD therapy (methotrexate plus sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine) results in better radiographic progression outcomes than methotrexate monotherapy, but the benefit is modest and not consistently larger than biologic intensification; in many patients, the clinical significance is limited over one to two years. <cite id="25992914,27571502,27102806,23755969,27607411">Triple therapy reduces radiographic progression versus methotrexate alone, while biologic add-on can be marginally superior, and overall effects on joint damage over 1–2 years are generally small</cite>.
